concepts.shortDescription: Generating and evaluating concrete move sequences.
Short forcing patterns that create immediate concrete consequences.
Longer-term coordination, plans, and positional decisions.
Recurring pawn configurations and their strategic consequences.
General principles for coordinating the initial phase of a game.
Techniques and decisions in materially reduced positions.
A repeatable process for understanding a position and choosing a move.
Generating a manageable set of plausible moves before calculating variations.
Identifying checks, captures, and direct threats that constrain the opponent's replies.
Maintaining an accurate mental representation of positions reached during calculation.
Following relevant variations far enough to evaluate their resulting positions.
Checking a calculated choice for tactical flaws and omitted alternatives before committing.
Actively searching for the opponent's strongest defensive and counterattacking possibilities.
One piece or pawn attacks two or more targets at the same time.
A piece is constrained because moving it would expose a more valuable target or illegal king attack.
An attacked valuable piece moves and exposes a less valuable target behind it.
Moving one piece reveals an attack by another piece, sometimes with check.
Forcing a defending piece away from a square, line, or duty it must protect.
Inducing a piece onto a square where a tactical consequence becomes possible.
Vacating a square, rank, file, or diagonal so another piece can use it.
Blocking the connection between a defending piece and what it protects.
Exploiting a piece that cannot fulfill all of its defensive responsibilities.
Eliminating or displacing a key defending piece before exploiting the target it guarded.
Playing an urgent intermediate move before completing an expected sequence.
Exploiting a king restricted by its own pieces on the back rank.
Coordinating threats that progressively restrict the king into an unavoidable mating attack.
Improving the scope, mobility, and useful influence of one's pieces.
Recognizing squares that cannot be adequately defended by pawns and may become stable targets.
Using a protected advanced square where a piece cannot easily be challenged by enemy pawns.
Using files with few or no friendly pawns as routes for rook and queen activity.
Using controlled territory to increase mobility and restrict opposing pieces.
Maintaining threats that require the opponent to respond and limit their freedom of action.
Anticipating and restricting the opponent's intended plan before pursuing one's own.
Evaluating whether a piece exchange improves the resulting activity, structure, or endgame.
Using a pawn advance or capture to alter lines, space, or structural tension.
Evaluating and improving the king's shelter, escape squares, and exposure to attack.
A central queen pawn without friendly pawns on adjacent files, creating both activity and weakness considerations.
Adjacent pawns on open files without neighboring pawn support, often trading mobility for targets.
A pawn that cannot safely advance and is difficult to support with neighboring pawns.
Two friendly pawns on the same file, changing mobility, control, and target structure.
A pawn with no opposing pawn able to stop it on its own file or adjacent files.
A numerical pawn advantage on one wing that may create a passed pawn or space gain.
Advancing fewer pawns against a larger pawn group to create structural targets.
Bringing pieces from their starting squares into useful play efficiently.
Influencing central squares to support mobility and restrict the opponent.
Securing the king while accounting for open lines and development.
Valuing each move as an opportunity to develop, control space, or address a concrete need.
Developing pieces so they support one another and contribute to a coherent position.
Sequencing principled moves to preserve options and limit undesirable replies.
Recognizing when early queen movement loses time or exposes the queen to development with tempo.
Using the king as an active attacking and defensive piece in reduced material.
Using direct king alignment to control entry squares in pawn endings.
Identifying king-access squares that determine whether a pawn can promote.
Using a three-move king maneuver to lose a tempo and transfer the move to the opponent.
Advancing, supporting, and restraining passed pawns in reduced material.
Prioritizing active rook placement, open lines, checks, and access to both wings.
Placing a rook behind a passed pawn to support its advance or restrain it from behind.
Building a bridge to convert the standard winning rook-and-pawn ending.
Defending the standard rook-and-pawn ending with third-rank activity and checking distance.
Determining what the opponent currently threatens before selecting a plan or move.
Comparing material, king safety, activity, structure, space, and concrete factors in the current position.
Choosing a coherent objective that follows from the evaluated needs of the position.
Updating the evaluation and plan after each move changes the position.
Allocating thinking time according to decision difficulty, clock state, and remaining game demands.

evidenceTypes.description: A mover-relative centipawn loss detected by a versioned engine analysis.
A severe mover-relative centipawn loss detected by a versioned engine analysis.
A meaningful engine-evaluated advantage was not retained by the played move.
A forced mate available before a decision was not preserved.
A decision changed the engine state to a forced mate for the opponent.
Engine MultiPV alternatives differ substantially, marking a consequential decision context.
A deterministic position rule or future classifier identifies a concrete tactical motif.
A deterministic position rule identifies a relevant structural feature.
A versioned decision classifier links a concrete decision to a concept and polarity.
A recorded attempt on an exercise explicitly targeting a concept.
A coach explicitly annotates evidence concerning a concept.
A structured assessment tied to a lesson or concept objective.
